title: Episode 160: Theodore Roosevelt: The Panama Canal, the Great White Fleet, and the Big Stick
description:
In his second term, Theodore Roosevelt strode across the world stage as a diplomatic and architectural titan. Frustrated by Colombian delays, TR backed a bloodless revolution in Panama, famously declaring: 'I took the Isthmus, started the canal, and then left Congress not to debate the canal, but to debate me.' He mediated the end of the bloody Russo-Japanese War in Portsmouth, New Hampshire—earning the Nobel Peace Prize—and dispatched sixteen gleaming white battleships of the United States Navy on an unprecedented fourteen-month circumnavigation of the globe. Discover the unapologetic audacity of TR's foreign policy: 'Speak softly and carry a big stick.'

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the global arena with Theodore Roosevelt. Armed with boundless energy and a vision of America as a supreme maritime power, Roosevelt redrew the physical geography of the planet by carving the Panama Canal and sent sixteen battleships around the world to show that the United States was ready to defend its interests anywhere on earth. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: 'SPEAK SOFTLY AND CARRY A BIG STICK'
In an address at the Minnesota State Fair in 1901, just days before McKinley's assassination, Vice President Theodore Roosevelt quoted a West African proverb that would define his entire philosophy of international statecraft: 'Speak softly and carry a big stick; you will go far.' Roosevelt despised empty bluster and theatrical threats. He believed that diplomacy was effective only when backed by visible, unhesitating military strength. In an era when European empires were carving up Africa and Asia, Roosevelt announced the 'Roosevelt Corollary' to the Monroe Doctrine in 1904.\n\nRoosevelt declared that chronic wrongdoing or impotence in Latin American nations would no longer invite European naval interventions; instead, the United States would act as an 'international police power' to maintain order, collect customs, and preserve hemispheric stability. While Latin American critics denounced 'gunboat diplomacy,' European chancelleries took notice. The young American republic was no longer a regional player, but a major maritime power whose national interests extended to every ocean on the globe.\n\nRoosevelt insisted that true international peace could be maintained only by nations that were capable of defending their own honor, rejecting disarmament as an invitation to aggression by predatory empires. In his view, a righteous nation had a duty to back its moral principles with tangible military readiness.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: 'I TOOK THE ISTHMUS'
For four centuries, explorers, merchants, and naval strategists had dreamed of cutting a canal through the narrow, mountainous isthmus of Central America to connect the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. The Spanish-American War had made the canal a military imperative: the battleship USS Oregon had been forced to steam fourteen thousand miles around the treacherous, stormy tip of Cape Horn from San Francisco to reach the Caribbean combat zone, taking sixty-eight agonizing days.\n\nWhen the Colombian Senate in Bogotá unanimously rejected a treaty leasing the canal zone to the United States, demanding more money, Roosevelt was beside himself with fury. Privately calling the Colombian politicians 'jackrabbits' and 'bandits,' Roosevelt quietly encouraged Panamanian rebels seeking independence from Colombia. In November 1903, Panamanian conspirators launched a bloodless revolution. Under Roosevelt's orders, American gunboats—including the USS Nashville—blocked Colombian troop ships from landing reinforcements. Three days later, the United States recognized the newly independent Republic of Panama, and signed the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty granting the United States a perpetual ten-mile-wide canal zone. TR famously proclaimed years later: 'I took the Isthmus, started the canal, and then left Congress not to debate the canal, but to debate me!'\n\nRoosevelt's swift recognition of Panama circumvented months of diplomatic stalling, demonstrating his unshakeable conviction that strategic necessity superseded legalistic delay. He viewed the canal not merely as an American asset, but as a monumental highway for global commerce.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: CONQUERING THE JUNGLE: DR. GORGAS AND JOHN STEVENS
Constructing the canal was the greatest engineering feat in human history. A previous French effort led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, the builder of the Suez Canal, had collapsed in catastrophic bankruptcy in the 1880s, claiming the lives of over twenty thousand workers to yellow fever and malaria. Roosevelt knew that modern science, not picks and shovels, would decide the canal's fate.\n\nRoosevelt backed Dr. William Crawford Gorgas, an army physician who accepted the revolutionary theory of Dr. Walter Reed and Carlos Finlay that mosquitoes transmitted yellow fever. Gorgas launched an unprecedented sanitation campaign across five hundred square miles of jungle, draining swamps, screening windows, and fumigating every building. In less than two years, yellow fever was wiped out entirely. Chief Engineer John F. Stevens abandoned the French dream of a sea-level canal, designing a colossal lock system and excavating the terrifying landslides of the Culebra Cut. In 1906, Theodore Roosevelt traveled to Panama, becoming the first sitting American president to leave the United States. Clad in a white linen suit and Panama hat, Roosevelt climbed into the cabin of a giant ninety-five-ton Bucyrus steam shovel in the pouring tropical rain, laughing with delight as he scooped up rock and dirt.\n\nUnder the leadership of Colonel George Washington Goethals, who succeeded Stevens, the Panama Canal project became a model of military engineering efficiency, overcoming mudslides, tropical deluges, and mountain excavation. Thousands of Caribbean laborers worked tirelessly under brutal tropical conditions to carve the great trench.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE PEACEMAKER OF PORTSMOUTH
While American steam shovels chewed through the mountains of Panama, a catastrophic war exploded on the other side of the globe. In 1904, the Russo-Japanese War erupted in Manchuria and the Yellow Sea. To the astonishment of European observers, the modernizing Japanese Empire repeatedly smashed the massive armies and fleets of Tsarist Russia, culminating in the complete annihilation of the Russian Baltic Fleet at the Battle of Tsushima in May 1905.\n\nYet both combatants were on the verge of exhaustion. Japan was financially bankrupt, and Russia was convulsed by the Revolution of 1905. Secretly approached by the Japanese Emperor, Roosevelt stepped forward as an impartial mediator. In August 1905, Roosevelt hosted Russian and Japanese envoys at the Portsmouth Naval Shipyard in New Hampshire. For thirty tense days, Roosevelt cabled the Tsar in St. Petersburg and the Emperor in Tokyo, hammering out compromises over territory and war indemnities. On September 5, 1905, the Treaty of Portsmouth was signed, ending the bloodiest war of the young century. For this brilliant diplomatic triumph, Theodore Roosevelt was awarded the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize—the first American ever to receive the honor.\n\nThe Portsmouth negotiations elevated American diplomatic prestige across Europe and Asia, proving that the United States could act as an impartial, disinterested broker in great-power conflicts. Roosevelt's tireless mediation earned him international acclaim as a master of modern statecraft.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE GREAT WHITE FLEET SETS SAIL
Despite the Portsmouth treaty, tensions between the United States and the victorious Japanese Empire escalated sharply over the status of the Pacific and racist school segregation laws targeting Japanese children in San Francisco. Japanese newspapers talked openly of war, and naval analysts questioned whether the American Pacific fleet could defend the newly acquired Philippines and Hawaii.\n\nTheodore Roosevelt decided to deliver an unmistakable visual demonstration of American naval power. In late 1907, Roosevelt ordered sixteen brand-new steel battleships of the United States Atlantic Fleet—their hulls painted gleaming white with gold scrollwork on their bows—to embark on an unprecedented fourteen-month, forty-three-thousand-mile circumnavigation of the globe. When pacifist senators threatened to withhold funding to keep the fleet at home, TR laughed in their faces: 'I have enough money to send them to the Pacific,' Roosevelt warned Congress, 'and if you don't appropriate the money to bring them back, they will stay there!' On December 16, 1907, Roosevelt stood on the deck of the presidential yacht Mayflower off Hampton Roads, Virginia, waving his hat as the sixteen leviathans fired thunderous 21-gun salutes and steamed out into the Atlantic.\n\nRoosevelt understood that a two-ocean navy was essential for American security, using the Great White Fleet's departure to shame Congress into funding additional modern dreadnoughts. He watched from the Mayflower with deep pride as the great white armada steamed out to sea.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: A TRIUMPHAL PAGEANT AROUND THE WORLD
The voyage of the 'Great White Fleet' was an unqualified international sensation. Commanded by Rear Admiral Robley D. 'Fighting Bob' Evans, the armada rounded the stormy Strait of Magellan, steamed up the coast of South America, and crossed the vast Pacific. At every port of call—Rio de Janeiro, Valparaiso, San Francisco, Auckland, Sydney, and Manila—hundreds of thousands of cheering citizens lined the harbors to marvel at the magnificent procession of American steel.\n\nThe critical diplomatic test occurred in Tokyo. Skeptics warned that the Japanese navy might launch a surprise torpedo attack. Instead, the Japanese government welcomed the fleet with overwhelming pageantry. Fifty thousand Japanese schoolchildren lined the streets of Yokohama waving American flags and singing 'The Star-Spangled Banner' in English. The display of peerless naval efficiency dissipated war rumors overnight and led directly to the Root-Takahira Agreement, in which both nations pledged mutual respect for their Pacific possessions and reaffirmed the Open Door policy in China. The fleet continued through the Indian Ocean, the Suez Canal, and the Mediterranean, completing its voyage without a single major mechanical breakdown.\n\nThe voyage tested the operational endurance of American naval engineering, disproving European critics who had predicted that the fleet would suffer catastrophic breakdowns in remote waters. In Australia and New Zealand, the fleet received an ecstatic welcome that strengthened Anglo-American ties.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE RETURN TO HAMPTON ROADS
On February 22, 1909—Washington's Birthday—the sixteen battlewagons steamed back into Hampton Roads, Virginia, their hulls stained by the salt of four oceans. President Roosevelt stood on the quarterdeck of the Mayflower, tears of pride streaming down his cheeks as the flagship Connecticut passed in review. Just ten days remained in his presidency.\n\nAddressing the assembled officers and sailors, Roosevelt declared with ringing conviction: 'Not another fleet of such size and power has ever made a voyage of that duration. The voyage was not a threat to anyone, but a message of peace and mutual respect. You have done a noble work for the United States, and every American citizen owes you a debt of gratitude.' Theodore Roosevelt had expanded the American navy from fifth in the world to second only to Great Britain's Royal Navy. He had proven that the United States could project decisive force to any corner of the planet, transforming a continental republic into an undisputed global superpower. He had spoken softly, carried the biggest stick in history, and changed the course of world events.\n\nAs the battleships dropped anchor at Hampton Roads, Roosevelt declared that the circumnavigation had permanently established the United States as a maritime power second to none. It was the crowning visual achievement of his presidency, leaving America secure and respected across the globe.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Theodore Roosevelt's foreign policy established the United States as an essential world power. By combining unapologetic military readiness with skilled diplomatic mediation, he maintained peace while securing the nation's strategic future. Next week, we examine the dramatic climax of TR's political journey: his bitter break with his handpicked successor William Howard Taft, the founding of the Bull Moose Party in 1912, and the miraculous day in Milwaukee when an assassin's bullet failed to stop a ninety-minute speech. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
